utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Hannis, is the Prosecution ready to continue the examination-in-chief of their present witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom. At the same time, I use the opportunity to first of all, and I'm now addressing the Defence, to express that it's my understanding that considerable progress has been made in the meetings with the Registry as far as communication and electronic media is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that there's still one thing over, that is, the laptop of Mr. Krajisnik in court. And I only wanted to convey to the Defence that the Chamber will further pay attention to that aspect. So in order to resolve that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Pasic, I apologise for dealing with other matters when you entered the courtroom. Good afternoon. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Yes. Then now Mr. Hannis will continue the examination. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic. When we left off yesterday, I believe we had just gotten to the point where your parents had decided to leave Vecici and they decided it would be best if you went with the group that your father was going with. And as I recall, you told us there were approximately 500 to 700 people in the group that you were travelling with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know how many people were in the group that your mother was going to go out with?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the total, but later on I found out that put into our buses from Grabovica the total of buses was 13 buses, all the civilians from Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how big the buses were, how many people were held on each bus? Were they full-size buses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say 50 to 60 people in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So could you tell the Court, please, then how you left Vecici in the group you went with. What time did you leave, and how did you go, and where were you heading?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 8.00 that night, when my father decided to take me to the safe place, Travnik, we left Vecici with a group of people. It was big. We were heading towards Jezica. It's the hill. And across to Travnik. Around 1.00 that night, we were approaching Jezica when we were ambushed by the Serbs for the first time, and as a result of ambush, two people died, Ahmet Zec and his son. I don't know his name. The group was separated in two, and I remember my father -- it was chaos, when he pushed me under this big tree and told me to stay there when this firing started. Approximately it lasted for 20, 30 minutes, and I didn't move. Then later he came back and he says -- he was calling my name: Elvedin, Elvedin, where are you? And I came out and he says: We have to move, we have to move. We were attacked. Then we joined this little group of people and we find out that other group left somewhere else. And then he says -- we found out that two people died and we need somebody to bury them and we need volunteers. At that time people were so afraid to go, and I know that two people left from that group, same group I was in. They took the bodies and buried them under a tree, just pushed them under the tree and covered them with branches. The same night, around 5.00, we joined the other group. We found each other. And we decided to walk, and we entered this open area. It was a field, clear. We were so tired and wet from the rain that we decided we're going to stay there and get some rest. I was so thirsty, I remember I told my dad: I need some water. Can you find me some water. He went out and he got me some water. And he -- when he came back, people running around and saying: We need to -- somebody needs to get up and go form the line, or go in the woods, look for Serbs. Nobody volunteered. Everyone was laying down. Nobody didn't care. Everyone just wanted to get some sleep. Then soon after that, we find out that the Serbs were surrounding us once again, and somebody just said: Get up, get up. We have to move now. And when we got up, that's when we were right in the middle of firing. I remember 15 to 20 men, young men, decided to stay and fight against Serbs. I followed my dad, and we were on this hill. We were going down the hill. Bullets were flying everywhere. In this group, we had a guy who knew the path towards Travnik. His name was Besim. He was from Vecici. There was a river dividing two hills. We were going down a hill and I had a huge coat, big coat. It was soaking in water. And I told my dad, I said: I can't move. I have to take this off. And he said: You have to move, we have to follow him. And I took my -- I said: I have to take it off. It's too heavy. And we stopped there, and when we stopped there we heard big bombs, mines exploded down there, you know, of this group in the river. Then he says: We have to move now. When we got there, ten people were dead from land mines. And this Besim guy who knew the path, he had his both legs blown off. And he was calling somebody to help him out, but we were so afraid, we had to cross that river, move on to the next side of this hill. Approximately 200 people of us all together. We paused for a minute there. We wanted to gather all together, figure out what we're going to do now. At the same time, we heard Serbs calling on megaphones: Balija, you have to surrender now. If you surrender, you're going to survive. If you don't, you're all going to die, and then they started laughing. That was big chaos. People didn't know where to go. In this group I remember hodza from Vecici. He was with us when he said -- his favourite saying was: Child, children, let's pray. We gathered all together and we prayed there. He said -- they decided what we going to do when this guy got up, he says: We're going to surrender. And people were just at that time -- didn't know what to do and we started walking towards this tunnel approximately 15 -- 50 to a hundred metres long. It was wide. We entered there, and this guy, Zec, he was in Vecici. I remember him, seeing him when we were walking through the woods contacting somebody, and I was telling my dad: That guy is talking to somebody. Every time we stop he goes underneath a tree and then he pulls out -- I'm sorry. He pulls out -- he pulls out this microphone or - I don't know - radio and then he starts talking. And I was telling my dad: That guy is talking to somebody. And he says: No. You just keep on moving. We have to move. And then he was the one who jumped in when we were in the tunnel. He says: Don't worry anything. We're going to surrender. He took his shirt. He's a white shirt and he ripped it off, used a branch and walked out of the tunnel. And he left with this one guy. And he was gone for 15 minutes. When he came back, he says: Oh, everything is fine. We just need to surrender. They guarantee us we're going to live. When we were coming out of this tunnel we noticed the snipers on both the ends -- the end and beginning of this tunnel. There was no way for us to escape. And as we were coming out this tunnel, they told us: Whoever had weapons, raise your -- put the weapons above your head. And just walk slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many people were still in your group by the time you got inside this tunnel, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got inside this tunnel, we had approximately 200 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you came out, did those with weapons lay the weapons down?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told us: Weapons on left-hand side. When we -- some of the guys were holding weapons, they told us: Put the weapons on left-hand side and all your gold, money, anything that you have, put it on the right-hand side. And I remember my mom gave it to my father, all the money, because they were hoping -- and we were hoping that we going to go to the Travnik, be safe. And she gave all the money that she had to him, and the gold. So I seen -- when I was passing this -- you know, because we were walking one by one, slowly, I've seen a lot of money, mainly Deutschmarks, and gold, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did they tell you what would happen if they found anything on anybody after you had gone and laid down weapons and valuables?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us: You have to leave everything. If we find a needle, we're going to kill you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After you all had done this, where did you go or where were you directed to go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were coming to this open area, I noticed Serbs were coming out of the trenches and they were celebrating, firing in the air. They told us to lay down on this muddy ground. One by one we were faced down like this. We lay down and that's when I noticed -- we heard trucks coming with more soldiers. And they told us: Lay down. If anybody gets up, we're going to kill you, we're going to shoot you. I know it was muddy and raining that day, and we approximately were staying there for two hours, faced like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was your father with you in this group that came out of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My father was there. My uncle, my cousins, my neighbours, and I also saw Hamida's husband, Elvir Lihovic, who was there ten metres above me in that line-up that we were laying down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Hamida was your sister and Elvir is your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I go on with this, I want to follow up on something with Elvir. You mentioned that your sister had lived in Dabovci. Am I pronouncing that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dabovci, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you aware of what had happened in Dabovci before this event in Vecici and Grabovica? Were you aware of what had happened in that village? Did your sister or brother-in-law tell you about that prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got to Vecici, we wanted to see Elvir Lihovic, my mom, because we heard when we were in Garici that horrible things happened at Dabovci. But we wanted to hear from him because he was the only one who survived from the men Dabovci. I was in the room when he was -- he told my mom everything what happened, that one day these mad soldiers, Serbian soldiers walked in the village and told all the men in Dabovci together all -- gather them all together and took them outside the village into one vacant house or -- where they shoot them all and burned this house. I know -- and he told us how -- my mom asked him: How did you survive? He said his friend who lived right next to him, he says when they lined them up -- when they start shooting at his friend jumped on him and hugged him. That's how -- pushed him on the ground and he survived there. After they shoot them all, he says they threw bomb, hand-grenade in this room where they were all killed. And also they -- he says later on they burned it, and when they left, they broke the window when he escaped to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember him telling you what kind of building they were in where they were shot and where it was burned?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building was for cattles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when you were on the ground, lying face down, after you had surrendered, how long did you stay there, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened during those two hours?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these two hours, Serb soldiers were telling -- picking out -- they started picking out people from this group and asking questions. I remember I could recognise them by the voice. I couldn't see him, but he was my neighbour, Mustafa, when they told him: Get up. And they asked him questions: Who is in charge? Who is your commander? And he says: Besim. So where is Besim? He says: He got killed from mines, and they start laughing. He says: Why don't you call him, start calling him. So he was there for 10, 15 minutes calling Besim, his name. There were also calling people and saying just saying: Okay. You were the snipers, you were shooting our soldiers, and they were beaten. I remember also hodza from Vecici. I can recognise his voice because his favourite voice was: My child. Anything that he was saying, he was saying "my child." They started beating him because they were saying: You hodza, you're responsible for this. They beat up my father. He was laying right next to me when they told him: Get up. And they just started beating him. Most of the people never came back to the group but he did. He came back and he was screaming and calling my name. He says: Are you okay, are you okay? I said: Yeah, I'm fine. They told us if anybody gets up we're going to shoot you. Don't turn around. And I remember my uncle was -- he was shaking. He says: When they started with these trucks that they were parked on our right-hand side, they were coming and we were face down, and I remember my uncle saying: They're going to run over us. They were coming close to the group. And if anybody gets up, they shoot you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember if there was -- if there seemed to be any system to how they were picking people out of the group?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that they were just picking people. As they were coming in the trucks, more and more soldiers were just picking people from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember hearing if they asked your father any questions when they had him get up?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember saying something about boots. Where did you -- I heard saying: Balija, where go did you get that boots? And he was saying: These are my boots. I was a hunter. They were saying: No, no. You killed our soldiers. You got our boots from him. He says: No. I was a hunter. And they started beating him. I can hear him in the background screaming. But he did came back to this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So after about two hours, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told all the women and children: Get up and start walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you get up at first?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first I refused, because I didn't know where we're going. And my father was -- he told me: Get up. Get up. And I says: No. Then my uncle says: Get up. You'll survive. And I was the last boy who got up from that group. They told us: When you get up, don't look around. Look in front of you. If you look around, we're going to shoot you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got up. I saw hodza. He was the only one who was faced this way. He was all in blood. I didn't see if he was moving or anything. I noticed he was all in blood. They told us to walk slowly and then at one time they told us to run and lay down and get up, towards Grabovica school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say hodza was laying "this way," you mean he was face up as opposed to everybody who was still face down?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How far did you have to walk to get to the Grabovica school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how far, but I know that we were going through the village and people were waiting outside, and mainly civilians and old people, spitting on us. I don't remember the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of Grabovica village, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened to you during the walk through the village to the schoolhouse?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I mentioned, when we were walking, we had civilians spitting on us, and I remember this, when this lady, female soldier, was walking by and she said: Does anybody got a match? Because she was holding a cigarette. And nobody didn't want to respond. She said: What's the matter, balija? Oh, that's right. You don't have anything now. And then they offered us a few times -- they told us to run, and lay down, crawl, and get up, three or four times, until we reached the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was escorting your group to the school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many women and children were there in this group that you were going to the school with, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately ten women, five to six boys, and I know we had injured guy who was carried with this female. He lay on the mine, and he was probably approximately - I don't know - 20 years old. And when he got up from the group, they told him: You're old enough to get up. We asked boys and females. And he was like -- they told him that -- he landed on the mine and they did -- they told him just to walk. I remember he was in that group with us too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened once you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, we were lined up on back yard where I guess students used to play basketball. And it was getting kind of dark, still raining, when this guy, accompanied with two, I guess, bodyguards, came towards us and introduced himself, but I don't recall his name. And he asked us -- he told us: Good evening. And he had some kind of hat with a light on, similar to a miner's hat. I remember seeing that. And he was in camouflage uniform. He told us that we're going to spend the night in the school and that nothing is going to happen to us, that tomorrow two buses will arrive and take us to Vrbanjci with the rest of the refugees and go safe to Travnik area. And he also says: All the men who left over, they're going to pay for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he say what "this" was that they were going to pay for?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember him saying: They're going to pay for all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How was this man dressed? Was he in civilian clothes or uniform?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any kind of insignia or rank?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed insignia and also I noticed on his shoulders he had stars and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did they do with you, women and children then?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to the school, and this school, in a classroom. The school had -- I call it two levels, the ground level and the top. They put us in this classroom. We were sitting there with two armed soldiers, sitting in a teacher's desk. One of then them was later on a guy who was captured in Vecici. He was fully armed. He was sitting in front of us and saying: Yeah. I was in Vecici. I was captured there. And then when he turned around, he saw this young girl who he recognised later on that started talking that they were going to school together. She was originally from Skender Vakuf. And he told her, he says: What are you doing here? She said -- she started crying: I visited my family in Vecici and that's how I ended up. He said: Don't worry. Nothing's going to happen to you. He brought her water, candy, and they offered us water too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The men in your group that had been left behind lying on the ground when you went to the school, did you see them again?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 10.00, 11.00 that night, I know it was really raining outside, really hard, when we -- we were looking through the window. We saw a man coming, walking in front of the trucks. That's the only way we saw them is just because they had these lights, and they were in front of trucks tied up, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "like this," can you describe where you saw them tied so it appears on the transcript. We can understand what you're --

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had -- they were tied with the wire around their wrists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these were the older men in your group that had been in the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened with them at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard them going upstairs into a classroom, and later on Serbs offered whoever wants to see their relatives, that they can go, raise the hand, and that we were free to go. I remember Hajrija Dugonjic who was married to the guy who was in Vakufci. She was the first one who wanted to go, and she was accompanied with two armed soldiers, took her upstairs. She saw -- when she came back, she told us she saw her husband beaten up, black and blue, and that he gave her a sign. So she asked him: Everybody there, she somehow -- he got her sign saying at that time everyone was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone else in your group of women and children go up to see the men?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gal from Skender Vakuf, she went upstairs to see her relatives. She came back and she was crying. She was saying the same thing, that they were all safe. I didn't want to go because when they -- when I was lying down with my father, they were asking him questions about boots and they also asked him: Do you have anybody in this group? And he says: -- At that time he says no. So that's why I didn't want to go, because I was afraid if I show up and if they see him, he might get killed or I might get killed. Nobody else, just two gals went upstairs to see them and nobody else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next morning, soldiers came in and they told us that we have to leave. Buses arrived. We've seen them through the windows. He says -- the soldier told us: Walk slowly to this fence. There was a little fence as you go school, and they're you're going to stop all together, and we're going to let you walk one by one, slowly. We're outside. Two rows of women and children were waiting outside for us, kind of formed a gauntlet where we had to go through, and he told us -- I remember clearly him saying: If you survive this, you will survive. They were holding axes, wooden sticks, pitchforks, and waiting for us to walk through. Everyone refused to go first, and I remember I was pushing towards this back fence. And this boy who was going to school with me, approximately my age. He says: I'll go first. And he started walking. As he got to the middle, somebody hit him so hard that he just fell and hit his knees. He couldn't move. He started crawling. Then he was -- as he was crawling, he was beaten in the back with the hands. And as we were passing by, everyone was trying to grab him and kind of push him towards these buses. There were approximately 100, 200 metres away from us. I was the last one who left the school, and I was beaten in my back. I was trying to rush through, but they told us: If you start running, we're going to shoot you. So I was about to reach the bus when this woman in a black -- dressed in black grabbed me and pushed me on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Take your time.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was holding a knife. She said: Let me kill this little balija because two of my sons died in Vecici. I was trying to get away, but she was so strong. Then this soldier who was standing right next to the door pushed her aside and literally grabbed me and threw me in there, in the bus, and closed the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to take a short break?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They closed the door, and somehow the buses didn't stop right away. And all these angry people that were waiting outside. They came around the buses, and they were spitting, throwing stones approximately for 15 minutes. They told us not to look around, outside. We might get hurt. I was laying down like this in front of seats, and all of a sudden buses stopped -- started, and we turned around and somebody from the second floor school...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second floor was where the men had been taken the night before?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see your father again after that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or your brother-in-law?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody from that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember about how many people were on the one bus that you got on?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 15 to 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say there were two buses?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. During the time that you stayed at the school that night, in addition to the group of women and children that you were in, did they bring in any other women and children during that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Where did you go once the buses started and left Grabovica school?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us we're going to Vrbanjci, where we're going to accompany 11 or 10 more buses, civilians from Vecici and surrounding villages, and that we're going to go to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you got to Vrbanjci, what happened?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we got there, they told us not to get out, and buses were already loaded, and I guess they were waiting for us. Approximately 12 to 13 buses total, and we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did that convoy of 12 or 13 buses go from Vrbanjci?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went across Vlasic Brdo to Travnik, and that's when we actually -- they topped us at Smetovi and told us to get out. That's when I met my mom, actually -- when I saw my mom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was she?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was in the buses in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after you got off the buses, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when we got off the buses, they told us to go. It was just chaos. All the civilians were just one huge group of people, going towards Travnik. And as we were walking, I remember seeing a lot of clothes, bags, leftovers, I guess, from the people before us who crossed there, who were going through there. It was hard to see roads. We were actually walking on the clothes. And as we were walking, I remember seeing masked soldiers jumping from the side of the road and asking for anything, money, gold, once again, stripping everybody, looking for money and gold. That happened like three or four times until we finally reached the end of it and the Bosnian side. An army was waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After -- once you got to the Bosnian side, did you have a chance to talk with your mom about what had happened to her, where she had gone after you left Vecici, and how she ended up being on a bus in the same convoy as you?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when we got to Travnik in this school, gymnasium school, she was surprised to see me. She said: What are you doing here? Aren't you with Dad? I said: Something horrible happened, I said. We all surrendered. She said -- she started crying and everybody asked: So what happened, what happened? And we told them that we were attacked and we had to surrender and that Serb soldiers told us: As long as we surrender, we're going to be fine. And she -- I asked her how -- what happened with you? Did anybody get hurt? She said: No. That night when we left Vecici, the following morning, they just walked all the civilians from Vecici straight across the bridge to Vrbanjci with white flag and they surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like now to show the witness an exhibit. And I'm not going to show him the next one I had on the list, which was a Crisis Staff document. But I want to show a November 4th combat report. The English is ERN 00892564.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit number P351.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I just want to read a part of the first paragraph and ask you a question about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, this is a combat report from the 1st Krajina Corps command to the Srpska Republika Army Main Staff dated 4 November and its number is 44-1/458.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, information on the enemy says: "Green Berets pulling out of Vecici village fell into our ambush. 40 of them were killed during the clash, and another 20 members of the so-called BH army were captured. Another 150 members of Green Berets, mostly women and children, surrendered in the evening hours." My question for you, Mr. Pasic: Were you a member of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you carry any weapons or engage in any fighting during this whole time you've been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about your mom or any of the other children and women in the group you were with?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I next would like to show the following exhibit, which is also a combat report from the 4th of November. The ERN of the English is 00892575.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Prosecution Exhibit number P352.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Pasic, I want to direct you to the second paragraph under number 2. And the number of this report is 44-1/459. The second paragraph reads: "In the area of Kotor Varos, there was a clash between members of Muslim forces and our units because of the refusal to negotiate on moving out of the Vecici village area. About 40 Green Beret members were killed and about 200 were captured. A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade." Was there any other group of soldiers that size leaving the Vecici village area at that time other than the one that you were with, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion as to whether or not this refers to your father's group?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that question. The witness answered "I don't know" in relation to the last question, and I don't think that Mr. Hannis's question can take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask a different question, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. And before the witness answers that question, if Ms. Loukas would have an objection, that would come first before the answer. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us when you left the village with your father's group, that that included most of the fighters, as I understood; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your mother remained behind and walked out of the village with a group of women and children?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any third group out of Vecici village?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We can set that document aside, and I want to ask you about one more. The next document, if we can give it a number. This is a combat report dated the 5th of November, and the English ERN is 01906052.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P353.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pasic, I want to direct you to paragraph number 4. Let me read a little bit and ask you a question. It says: "The situation in Kotor Varos municipality is still very complex. After they refused to return the weapons and surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska, Muslim extremists from the village of Vecici attempted to fight their way through towards Travnik. In the clash against the Army of Republika Srpska, following the death of one soldier and wounding of several others, more than 150 extremists died in combat." At the time you left the Grabovica school, when the soldiers -- the men from your group were up on the second floor, were they already disarmed?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And bound with wire on their wrist?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not engaged in combat at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm loath to object, of course, but that little last series of leading questions should be avoided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the question whether people bound by their wrists and disarmed were engaged in combat is rather a comment than a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, are you ready to start cross-examination or would you, in view of the time, we'd still have perhaps first have a break. Perhaps -- I don't know whether the witness would prefer to have an early break and then be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence, or whether you'd prefer to continue for another half an hour. I don't know how much time you would need, Ms. Loukas, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, my cross-examination won't be that long, but I think in view of the emotional nature of the evidence in chief, it might be appropriate for a short break before I proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. We could have a break now for approximately some 20 to 25 minutes and then you'll be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas. But if you'd prefer to continue now, then we could do that as well. Could you tell me what your preference is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Loukas. You'll be cross-examined by Ms. Loukas, who is counsel for the Defence. Ms. Loukas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, you've obviously been through a lot and your evidence, I think, has been very emotional for you. I can indicate that I'll keep my cross-examination as short as possible, and hopefully most of the questions I'll be asking you are capable of a very short yes or no answer. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I think you gave a statement back in December 2000 in relation to the matters that you've given evidence of?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. You gave a statement in December 2000 in relation to the matters that you've been giving evidence of yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And that's a statement, obviously, that's true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you were given an opportunity at the time you gave the statement to read through it and make any corrections if they were required?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And when coming to The Hague on this occasion to give evidence, obviously you went through the statement with the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And he gave you an opportunity to correct the statement if there were any need to correct it?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to take you through some matters that are contained in your statement, very briefly. Obviously, you gave your statement very carefully, and of course you gave your evidence yesterday and today very carefully. But there's just a couple of matters from your statement that didn't come out in full, and I'd just like to take you through them. Are you with me?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, would you prefer the English copy or the B/C/S copy?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: English copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have other copies of the English statement and the B/C/S statement, but there may not be any need. I just propose to read out small sections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can have them ready and available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be -- if we have two copies, one to be put on the ELMO, the other for the witness, both two English copies, so that everyone can follow it and that the witness has a copy, which is easier than --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I do have additional copies if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It depends. It also depends on whether the Prosecution considers that anything is taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Need more, if not, we do not hear from the Prosecution, we'll just do it as you suggested.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, instruct her which page to put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, firstly, just going to page 3 of the statement, and that would be the paragraph fourth from the bottom of page 3. Do you see the paragraph I'm talking about, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And do you notice a sentence there in about the middle? It says -- this is in reference to that meeting that occurred in your house around the time of Bajram in 1992. And this sentence -- these two sentences here: "They verbally started to count names of persons who had weapons. My father was a hunter and owned a licenced hunting gun." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just going on the page 4 of your statement. This is about your arrival in Bilice, which was the -- a Croat village. And just the portion contained in that last paragraph there: "It was well organised and the locals had dug trenches around the village in preparation to defend themselves against a Serb attack. When we arrived in the village, I saw around 50 armed men in the trenches, around 15 to 20 of them wearing camouflage uniforms and wore some Croat symbols. The others were in civilian clothes." That is, of course, correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You go on to say there that: "Most of the men carried hunting guns; however, some had automatic weapons too. When we arrived in Bilice, all military-aged men from my village, including my father and brother, were already there." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Additionally, if you go down a little further in the paragraph, the sentence commencing: "During this one-month period some military-aged men from Hrvacani assisted the Croats." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you also go on to mention there that: "The others from our village went in the direction of Vecici," and they included your father, your brother; Nihad Pasic, your cousin; Sefik Pasic, your uncle; Mehmedalija Pasic, another of your cousins; Sakib Pasic, another of your cousins; Ibrahim Pasic, a cousin; Mustafa Pasic, a cousin; Redzo Pasic, a neighbour; and his son Jasmin Pasic. Alija Pasic, a neighbour; his four brothers, Refik, Alija, Fazil, and one whose name I don't recall but I know he was one of the persons killed in Vecici. Muradif, son of Murat Dugonjic" -- sorry. Am I going too fast? "And many others whose names I don't recall now. This group consisted of around 50 men." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just going on to page five of your statement, just down to the third-last paragraph, and you're dealing there in your statement with when you came back to your village and in fact to your own home and saw that it had been destroyed. You indicated there in the I think third-last paragraph, the last sentence: "I believe Serb friends of my brother who had gone to school with him and knew that my brother was in the military did this." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just in relation to page 6 of your statement, the last paragraph there, you're dealing with coming to Garici. Do you see that paragraph that I'm talking about there?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you there refer to a woman who was -- I think you've indicated there -- I think this was a Serb woman in the village, and I think you've given evidence of this nature today. But the situation was that the -- this distraught woman who approached, the soldier told her to move away; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: From what you could see, he was trying to protect you in that instance; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the next page, page 7. That's the last sentence of the first paragraph. This is at the time that you were staying in the house of Atif Agambegovic. You stayed in this village, you state in the statement, for about a month. And you also indicate there in that last sentence that: "This was around July 1992." And you state there that: "During this period my father or brother did not visit us." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just moving on to the next page, at page 8 of your statement. You're referring there to some days spent in Vecici, where you were in the cellar, and then you're referring there to your father coming back. If you look at the third paragraph there, this is in relation to that discussion about whether you should stay with your mother or go with your father. What you have there is: "They discussed the option of whether I should stay with my mother and go to Travnik with the convoy or instead accompany my father and the other fighters who were going to attempt to escape through the woods." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, you've also I think given evidence yesterday and today that in terms of the numbers of people who left, it was 500 to 700 people, mainly men, three females, and 15 boys; correct? That was the evidence that you gave in court yesterday, just before we finished. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said approximate.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, approximately, yes. Now, there in your fifth paragraph on page 8, you indicate, of course, that the group was quite big, and you also indicate there that it comprised of all the fighters and some children and about ten women; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, just going to page 9 of your statement. And this is something you gave evidence of today. This is the second-last paragraph on page 9. You referred to this officer and you referred to it in this statement as well. It's the last part of your second paragraph from the bottom, in relation to the officer at Grabovica school. This officer was in camouflage uniform. Do you see the portion of your statement that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: "He said: Hey, how are you doing. Then he told us his name, which I don't recall. Then he said," and this is the quote you have in your statement: "You women and children will go to the school and then tomorrow you will go to Travnik. I guarantee that nothing will happen to you." Then he continued: "You have no guilt whatsoever. You'll go to the school, but your fighters will pay for whatever happened. He then left." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And you also refer in that very last paragraph to -- this is the second sentence, two or three later -- "Two or three hours later our fighters were also brought to the school and the group of fighters were taken upstairs." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just going to the very last page of your statement. Again, this is a reference to at that stage when you were trying to get on the bus, and this woman said that she was trying to kill you. And she said: "My two sons were killed at Vecici." You remember that portion, of course. And it was the situation that the soldier actually came and pushed the woman aside so that you could get on the bus; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And again, from what you could see, the soldier was trying to protect you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, just going to your stays in these various villages that you've given evidence of. It's correct, is it not, that those villages, and I include in that Cirkino Brdo, Hanifici, Garici, and Vakufci, those -- and please, if my pronunciation is not conveying the names, please let me know. But it's your understanding, is it not, that those villages in the local area that gave up their arms and signed the loyalty oaths, that they would not fight with the Serbs, those villages were actually safe for the people who lived there; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You also gave some evidence of having heard about some people being killed at a hospital. This was something that you'd heard. Do you recall the bit of evidence that I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have a page reference. I don't remember mentioning a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, actually, I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it yesterday's transcript? Then we could search for the word "hospital" and see whether there's any "hospital" in it. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now that you say that, Your Honour, I think there was with regard to -- he was talking about events in Vecici, when a group of Serbs broke through the lines and then I think he mentioned the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll find that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, you're invited to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's just a little difficult because the laptop is a long way from the microphone. But I could use this microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The bit of evidence I'm talking about, Mr. Pasic, is -- yes, I think this was information that you'd heard from others that they entered the village, they broke the line, they got there and they burnt 30 houses and killed everyone that was there and even a hospital that we know. Because my cousin was in the hospital and he survived from the hospital when they came to kill everybody, and he was telling us how everything -- Do you see the portion that I'm talking about? Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, obviously it's correct that you don't have any idea about what was going on immediately, no direct knowledge, of course, no direct knowledge about what was going on immediately before they were killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Can you -- can you rephrase that question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm happy to do that. What I'm dealing with here is you understand the difference between something that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel kindly speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- something you saw for yourself, as opposed to something you heard from someone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: You understand that distinction? And that's the distinction that I'm making there. So it's a relatively simple question, and it's just that you have no direct knowledge as to what actually occurred in relation to that incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean by the incident, the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: The hospital incident, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I think you also indicated earlier in your evidence yesterday that when you were in your village that you saw some Serb soldiers, and one particular Serb soldier seemed to be very agitated and was saying: There is no place for you here. But the -- you said the other soldier was very kind and asked you nicely: What are you doing here? Do you recall that part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And in fact, I think that he offered you two soldiers so that you could go to Garici; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And one of those soldiers who accompanied you in fact tried to -- well, in fact did protect you from an angry Serb woman; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I just need to check something from today's transcript, and I just need ten seconds to do that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, just in relation to some questions that the Prosecutor asked you today. Do you recall being asked this question in relation to a document that you were shown: "Was there any other group of soldiers that size leaving the Vecici village area at that time other than the one that you were with, if you know?" And your answer was: "I don't know." That's at page 20 of the transcript today, for the benefit of Your Honours and the Prosecution, and that's in reference to Prosecution Exhibit number P352. Now, you remember that question and answer, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: And later on, Mr. Hannis, a few questions later, asked you this question: "Was there any third group out of Vecici village?" And your answer was: "No, sir." Do you remember that answer, those two answers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it, in essence, that what you're saying there is that you actually don't know; to your knowledge, there wasn't, but you don't know for certain. I guess that's basically the import of what you're trying to get across there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say: In the group that I was with 200 people, when we got ambushed, I don't know what happened on that hill. I don't know how many people left there. I know 15 to 20 people, armed soldiers, young boys, decided to fight Serbs. Like I mentioned before, that long group, I don't know what happened to the rest of the people, but the group that I was in, we left towards Grabovica. I don't know what happened up there. First of all, we thought everyone got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's basically your answer in relation to that aspect of your evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Mr. Hannis, is there any need to put any further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I have a few questions to you, some of them just being requests for clarification

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just answered a question of Ms. Loukas, saying that you did not observe yourself the incident at the hospital of which you told us and which you learned about through your aunt. Your testimony about the hospital is embedded in what you said you observed from Cirkino Brdo, when Vecici was attacked. You said that you saw 30 houses burned. And you told us about using binoculars. You observed the burning of those houses when the forces entered Vecici yourself, even if at a distance?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. We were -- at that time I remember clearly that was I believe third day of the air striking when we were at Cirkino Brdo. As I mentioned before, we watched them entering Vecici village from that side. It was clear to see it, because there was an opening and when they entered the village, we saw the smoke coming from the houses, and later on firing started, and like 20 to 30 minutes later on we saw them coming, running through the field back to Vrbanjci. And that's when we noticed that -- we were crying. As a matter of fact, I was right next to my mom. She was crying and saying: Oh, my god. They're going to kill them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you see from that distance that these were Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the binoculars, clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I have one question in relation to the arms. You told us that you had to disarm when you left the tunnel, when you surrendered. Could you give us an indication on what type of weapons there were, and also the quantities. Because you testified that at an earlier stage, that there was hunting rifles and a few automatic weapons. That was a few stages before that. What kind of weapons were still available to the group when you left that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned before, Your Honour, my dad was a hunter, and I remember he had a gun and a hunting gun. When we left that tunnel, mainly with pistols, I remember that, and hunting guns, and I believe a few automatic weapons. When they -- I did not see them, but once the men, they rised them up in the air, that's when I saw them. And my dad, I remember seeing him putting the gun on the left-hand side. That's what they told us, to put them down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us: Did all men, apart perhaps from the children or the boys, did they all carry arms?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you tell us approximately what percentage. Was it one out of two, one out of four, one out of six?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, in my opinion, out of 200 people that were in the tunnel, no more than 15 to 20 had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you also tell us what weapons the Serb soldiers had who you were ambushed by?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when we were coming out of tunnel, we found a mistake and a M-48 was used to -- they were firing above our heads. Four of them sitting in the trench. I remember that clearly. Mainly automatic weapons, and also hand-grenades. Because when we were on this side of the hill they were above us, because we could hear them talking on the megaphone. They started throwing hand-grenades down because they saw us coming, and as a matter of fact I believe they knew that we were going to go this way because like I mentioned we had a guy who was collaborating with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a question of a totally different nature. I noticed that going back to this period of your life, of course, made you very emotional. Did you ever receive any professional help in overcoming what you experienced at that time?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. But I know, last night, these past two nights I've been dreaming again, and even my wife, you know, saw me jumping. It's hard when you go back and experience that. I know I was really sick first two months when we escaped to -- I had that truck in my mind every time I go to bed and I'd wake up: They're going to run over us. I had that picture in my mind and it was hard to get it out of it. But, you know, life now moves on, and I'm in America, you know, busy life. And every time I go back to this and start thinking about this, it brings back a lot of memories and I have nightmares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you never received any psychiatric or psychological treatment. Do you take any medication in order to suppress those bad moments?

utterances.speaker: ELVEDIN PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these answers. Do they trigger any need for further questions by the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, as I told you before, of course the Chamber has observed how emotional it was for you to go back to a period of your life and to testify about it, just as you also explained in the answer to my last question. The Chamber very much appreciates that you came, that you testified, that you answered the questions of both parties and of the Bench, and we wish you a safe trip home again, and also strength, because what you testified about, if you have gone through such an experience, you need strength for the future. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pasic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before I ask Madam Registrar to assist us, I would have one procedural issue I'd like to raise, which doesn't take me any more than two or three minutes. We could do that after the break. We could read some 92 bis statements into the transcript. Are there any other issues we would have to discuss?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. There is a procedural issue that I would wish to raise, but it's an issue that I can raise after the break. And I note the time. I think it's -- it is the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's the time for the break now. I just wondered if it was just a matter of two minutes and if we would not have to come back, then of course we could deal with it. But we have still so much on our agenda that we'll have a break now. We'll adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, perhaps we first start with the most recent matters, and that is, exhibits in relation to Mr. Pasic. Madam Registrar, could you assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P349, photograph of a damaged mosque. P350 and 350.1, extraordinary session of the War Presidency. P351 and P351.1, combat report to Srpska Republica, number 441/458. P352 and 352.1, combat report to Republika Srpska army, number 441/459. P353 and 353.1, combat report to the Main Staff dated 05 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There's no objection to the documents that have been indicated. I will just place one matter on the record, and that is that there is a translation issue in relation to one of the documents. That's P350. And Ms. Cmeric has already conveyed the particular aspect that's in dispute to Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we'll -- Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I have been given that document, and just based on my review of it, I think the changes suggested by the Defence are correct, even though it is a CLSS translation. The same word in B/C/S is translated different in one place and it seems to me it would make sense to use the same English word in all places it appears. We will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Unless of course sometimes the context asks for different translations, but I'll leave that to you and the CLSS. So I take it you'll finally make up your mind and that you'll provide us with a new copy of 350.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may have noticed that Madam Registrar has shortened a bit the description of the exhibits. Not on paper, but she reads as far as necessary in order to identify the documents as unique documents, and you'll find very often a bit broader description on paper as we're used to. So then 349, 350, without translation, and then 351, up to and including 353, including translation, are admitted into evidence. And we get a new translation of 350, which then will bear the number 350.1. Yes, Ms. Loukas. There was another procedural issue you'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Always having issues with the microphone, I must say. Your Honour, Your Honours, just in relation to the statement of the witness who just completed his evidence that I used in cross-examination, Your Honours, I propose to tender the statement, in view of the fact that there were significant areas that I did cross-examine on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection. I take it, Ms. Loukas, that wherever you've drawn the attention of the witness to the parts, that's where the most important parts for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, I have, Your Honour. Indeed, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The others, although then in evidence, are not the most important ones for the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. I have the relevant documents here in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D30, thank you. And the original is English. Is there a B/C/S translation for it? That would then be D30.1. So that Mr. Krajisnik can read it in his own language. Ms. Loukas, if you would allow me just to make one short comment on the cross-examination. As you may have noticed, when you were about to object, you did not really object against Mr. Hannis. I told Mr. Hannis that some of the questions were rather comment than a question to the witness. Well, asking the witness to confirm that his testimony was what it was is also a comment to the extent that you indicated, that it's an important part of the testimony of the witness which is of course just as much I would say comment. Rather, it doesn't bring anything new. There was no need to stop you and you stayed within limits, but if the parties could refrain from putting by their own means the emphasis on what the testimony is, then -- and otherwise, one could even ask ourselves whether the parties could not say of major importance for us is that and that and that part. It's nothing else if you asked witness: Is that what you said? Yes, that's what I said. Okay. And of course the Chamber is aware that that's of importance for the Defence. Every piece of the testimony is important for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think I'll have to reread what Your Honour said before I can agree entirely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some parts you said: Was this your evidence? Then you repeated it literally, and the witness said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These were mainly issues the Chamber can imagine needs some special emphasis as far as the Defence is concerned. Yes. So that's to that extent it's mainly -- it's not asking a question to a witness but it's underlining the answer he gave already at an earlier stage of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: This is in relation to the Prosecution or to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both. You did it as well. That's why I try to make you share the -- no. You did it a couple of times, just asking: Was this your testimony? Yes, this was my testimony. There could be hardly any doubt on whether that was his testimony, just as, well, the one issue where I said it was rather comment than a question to the witness. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think I understand now, Your Honour. It's a generalised observation for both Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I was not clear enough, then at least you understood it by now. Is there --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There was a procedural issue I indicated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to an issue that from the Defence perspective has arisen particularly in relation to two of the witnesses called this week, for example, and it's a matter that I feel is appropriate to put forward a Defence perspective in relation to the procedures that are being adopted by the Prosecution. If one looks, for example, at Witness 144, the protected witness, his evidence was dealt with via 89(F). This was a witness who, Your Honour, in -- and I won't go into the nature of his position or of his evidence, of course, but this was a witness that one might have expected, and it would be appropriate to be called in terms of a -- on a viva voce basis. If one looks at the witness that we have just dealt with today, Mr. Pasic, that was a witness that could have been dealt with on an 89(F) basis or even conceivably on a 92 bis basis because the witness has given evidence previously, rather than bringing the witness all the way from his current country. Now, Your Honour, but I guess the main issue is the use of 89(F), where the Prosecution is exercising its discretion in relation to the use of 89(F). And for my part, I place before the Court the Defence's concerns in relation to the use of 89(F). The last witness, in my submission, would have been appropriate for 89(F) and need not have gone through his -- obviously very emotional evidence in this way, whereas the previous witness, Your Honour, in light of the nature of his evidence, would have been appropriate for viva voce testimony, in my submission. And I do place that marker there, and it is an area on which the Defence submits that the Trial Chamber should give some guidance to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you have any suggestion for that guidance? Because giving guidance is one, but ... I mean, because for one witness you say it should not have been 89(F), for the other it should have been. So guidance goes in two direction. Would you have any criteria in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, obviously the criteria go to the significance of the evidence in relation to what are the major issues in this case. And quite clearly, the sort of evidence given by the last witness, if we are to use the 89(F) procedure, is the sort of evidence that might be appropriate for an 89(F) procedure, whereas we would submit the sort of evidence given by 144 is not appropriate for 89(F), if one makes the comparison. And it was quite a stark example this week, and from the Defence perspective we wish to place that before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Especially you draw our attention to the significance of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll consider whether the Chamber will give some guidance as you requested to the Prosecution. We'll take some time to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. The other aspect, of course, is in relation to the reading of 92 bis summaries. One of the summaries proposed to be read today relates to the transcript, that is, Mr. Adil Draganovic, a witness from Sanski Most, who was dealt with under 92 bis. Now, Your Honour, there was the -- the significance of this is, of course, that this is not merely meant to be a summary of a statement, but what is put forward by the Prosecution is transcript from previous testimony. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I would submit that it's incumbent upon the Prosecution to also include a summary of the cross-examination. Just prior to Your Honours coming into court I raised this issue with both Mr. Gaynor and Mr. Hannis, because I said I objected to the reading of a summary of this nature when the material -- I mean, if these summaries are for the information of the public so that they know what sort of information is being tendered, where there's transcript being tendered, to merely summarise the evidence in chief, Your Honours, is in my submission inadequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if we want to inform the public about - or Mr. Gaynor - about what is in evidence, would you agree that testimony given in cross-examination would just be as important as in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's difficult for us to judge which portions of cross-examination should be summarised. One thing that we do do in looking at the cross-examination in a transcript and deciding what to put in our summary is that if an answer given or an explanation given in cross-examination, then cuts down from something that was said in direct examination, we're not going to put that direct examination statement in the summary. But I propose to Ms. Loukas that perhaps they want to write a cross-examination summary. Because I don't know that I'm going to be able to do a satisfactory job for the Defence of summarising what they think is important in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's, of course, we'll leave out from the summaries what's totally unimportant, but I think that -- first of all, the summaries could be relatively short. I was about to give an indication on what was the subject of the testimony. And isn't it true that counsel always should be aware of what is very important for the other party? So I would not accept that counsel were not in a position to see what the other party considers to be important. But again, these summaries are provided to the other party before being read in court. So if there's any need to introduce a specific element of the cross-examination, I take it that then the Defence will indicate so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to do that. I know with this particular witness that if I were on the Defence side, I suppose one point I would want to make about this witness is that there are some issues that bear on his credibility. For example, there were some allegations about his behaviour as a judge at some point in time. That might be important. But I don't know if that's something that needs to go in the 92 bis summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
