But, of course, this raises another matter, and that is to what extent the summaries should reflect -- perhaps it should - specific issues, questions raised in view of the reliability of that witness. Of course, that's very difficult to summarise that, because you quickly would come to a point where you are taking position on whether a certain answer is an indication of unreliability or not. We'll give it some thought, and perhaps for the witness just discussed, perhaps the parties could sit together so that that statement would not be read or, if they have already agreed upon it, that it could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that event, Your Honour, perhaps we won't read this one today and save it for a later occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And see whether the suggestions of the Defence could be followed. Ms. Loukas, is there --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. There's one further remaining procedural matter. Your Honours will recall on the last housekeeping day, on the 4th of October, I raised the issue of the diary of a witness who gave evidence in late May of this year. And it was indicated by the Prosecution that they were in possession of that diary and had been in possession of that diary, for some time, and had not conveyed it to us. In the circumstances, Your Honour, I can indicate that on the 8th of October we received in court, and by e-mail, a statement of the relevant witness in relation to the diary. I would convey to the Court the Defence's dismay that something -- the statement, in fact, is dated the 2nd of July. Your Honour, that sort of delay in informing the Defence is entirely unacceptable. The fact is that the witness in question gave a declaration in relation to his -- sorry. The investigator, sorry, gave a declaration in relation to the diary in Banja Luka on the 3rd of June. This sort of delay in conveying information to the Defence - that is, from June and July until October - is, as I've indicated, Your Honour, unacceptable from the Defence perspective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not the diary that still had to be copied, or is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a diary that was to be conveyed to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- but it first had to be copied. Isn't that -- or am I now confusing two diaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think there's another diary you're thinking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is one that we have now provided the B/C/S -- a copy of this witness's diary to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis, the objection by the Defence is mainly about delays in delivering messages to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I have to take responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you accept the criticism as justified?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're all engaged in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your previous answers you take responsibility but it was not clear yet for what exactly. So the Defence -- the Prosecution accepts the criticism and I take it also will take care that it will not happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. As you recall, at that time we were all engaged in other matters that were keeping us very busy as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apologies accepted. I understood it as apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: It's important to be gracious at moments like these, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Loukas. Then any other procedural issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I have something, Your Honour. I'm perfectly happy for Mr. Hannis to go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we had time I was going to try and suggest we go through some exhibits on some previous witnesses, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're talking about 200 until 203 or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Still not ready on that one, Your Honour. Mr. Margetts's witness earlier in the week, 144, there were still a couple of matters. And for the witness from October 5th, KRAJ 191, Mr. Medanovic, his exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't been here all week. I knew you were missing me, and of course the other way around as well, Your Honour, naturally. But I've actually come for a specific purpose. Your Honour, I see my client of course in the course of this week, and particularly I went with Ms. Cmeric to see him this morning. And there is a practical issue, Your Honour, which I hope the Trial Chamber can help with. I mentioned it to Mr. Hannis just before we came into court. For the last two or three weeks, I think it is or something like that, we've been having discussions with the Registry in connection with the possibility of some members, not very many, but some members of the team of investigators out in Republika Srpska, Bosnia and Herzegovina, coming to The Hague to have discussions with Mr. Krajisnik and of course with members of the Defence team. It's clear that Mr. Krajisnik can't go to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From a practical point of view, it's also exceptionally difficult for the Defence team to find time to go to them as well. This is not been easy because there are all sorts of policies and practices and restrictions and so on, some of which have been very helpfully and very flexibly treated in relation to this situation. So that in principle, we do have approval for investigators to come and see Mr. Krajisnik out at the UN Detention Unit. But of course that raises the question of when. This discussions has been going on for some time. Mr. Krajisnik, with justification, we submit, is extremely anxious that this should happen as soon as possible, and we would have liked to set it up a little while ago, but there have been all sorts of hoops and hurdles and so on. So it's in a sense a little overdue anyway. This morning we considered and looked at what were the possibilities, and I should preface this, Your Honour, by saying we got to -- carts to come before horses and so on. We haven't got a confirmed date for the investigators to come, but we believe that they are pretty flexible and available at reasonably short notice. So I can't say we have a date. But, Your Honour, we do have a date in mind which I mentioned to Mr. Hannis, which I now raise with the Trial Chamber. And another point, I should mention it, it is not possible for the investigators to go and see Mr. Krajisnik at the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That might not be totally satisfactory anyway. It's a dead issue because it's simply not possible. It has to be during the week. I hope that Your Honours will see that from a practical point of view, for that to happen while the Trial Chamber is sitting on the case is also not really feasible. The hours they're left in the day and the energy left in the day and then the investigators are here in The Hague while Mr. Krajisnik is in court. So from a practical point of view, time is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- needed to do so. So Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had a date in your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Cutting to the chase, Your Honour, as we say: Specific dates that we did have in mind, subject to confirming, but we're reasonably confident about that, would be Thursday, the 4th, and Friday, the 5th of November. And there are a number of different reasons which would seem to fit together in a positive way, including the fact that -- and this I sprung it on Mr. Hannis a few minutes ago, but it seems that that also doesn't probably cause major disruption in terms of scheduling and witness availability as far as the Prosecution are concerned. And it does fit in as well as any other dates in a practical way and is quite soon. It's probably as soon as realistically can be managed without disruption to the Trial Chamber and everybody else. So, Your Honour, we do need to double-check, of course, that they could come that date. Otherwise there would be no point. But that's the position, Your Honour, and that's in principle our request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, two questions arise: The first one is whether it -- because we're quite close to that date, whether it would cause major problems to the Prosecution. If so, we'll have to see what to do. The second question is that these are two days that we're supposed to sit in court. Would the Defence agree that perhaps at a later stage during a period where we were supposed not to sit, that we have two additional days then so that it's budgetary neutral, as they say nowadays, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with -- I was very much hoping that Your Honour wouldn't take that attitude because this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not taking an attitude. I'm just asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, all right. I beg your pardon, Your Honour, if I was -- all right, I withdraw that. Your Honour is asking the question then. With respect, Your Honour, it's -- it fits in with the case but it is extra work, Your Honour. We really would strongly urge the Trial Chamber not then to try balance it with those days which are -- they're less than is needed, Your Honour, anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll understand in a couple of minutes from now on why perhaps I put this question at this moment. But so I do understand. Mr. Hannis, have you already considered the 4th and 5th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart did speak to me about this during the break. We do have witnesses scheduled for that week. Whether it's a major problem, it's always a problem because, you know, the witnesses react a certain way when they are scheduled and then they are rescheduled, and it has a cumulative effect. But it's less of a problem on those two days than some other days would be. But again, we would ask to consider the possibility of having this meeting during a time when we weren't going to sit anyway. But I don't know what the rest of the Defence's schedules are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the -- I would say the days that would first come into the mind of the Chamber might be the -- just the week after that. 4th and the 5th are a Thursday and Friday, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, they are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Friday the 12th is a UN holiday. Of course we would not sit -- if you would delay it for one week, it would fall well within the one sitting weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this this morning with Mr. Krajisnik. All I can say, I speak for Mr. Krajisnik, but I do certainly pass on his views. His reaction to -- in fact, I had suggested that following week first of all as a possibility, but Mr. Krajisnik's reaction was extremely negative, to a further delay of a week. And in fairness to Mr. Krajisnik, well, of course, I should above all be fair to Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But in fairness, this is an issue which has been already boiling along for several weeks while we tried to get the practical aspects sorted out. So -- and Your Honour, it's quite a tight -- Mr. Krajisnik wishes to have quite a lot of time with the investigators. It's quite a time-consuming matter for us, the Defence team, to participate in this exercise as well, and we are, Your Honour, faced with a really very heavy programme of witnesses coming up. I don't really submit there could be any serious argument about that. So I'm urging Your Honour to help us as much as possible in relation to the timetable and the dates and the availability of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention while I'm on my feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's slightly linked to this, although it's a separate point. It's this: That we hope that in all the planning and the scheduling by the Prosecution - in fact, we invite the Prosecution to have regard to this - that something could be borne in mind which may not be sufficiently appreciated until one actually comes across it in practice, which is this: For example, we have a witness coming up, if he is in fact allowed to give evidence at all. But we have a witness coming up later in November, subject to an application to give evidence. If he does, there is total of 235 pages of transcripts of interviews with that witness. There's another witness scheduled for the next few weeks who has 130 pages of transcript, and then there's another one who is scheduled, if he comes at all, to come rather later in the new year, but 200 and something pages. But several hundred pages of interviews. Mr. Krajisnik only has available to him in relation to those the English transcript and the B/C/S audiotape. And we discussed this with him this morning as well. Mr. Krajisnik is quite clearly, according to our assessment, under enormous pressure in relation to this case, and is already staying up well after midnight in order to work on this matter, and he has to be in court for five days and travel backwards and forwards. A rough calculation, Your Honour, is we believe, as best we can judge, interviews probably go at broadly the same pace as court proceedings. Court proceedings seem to produce about 20 pages of transcript an hour. So 235 pages of transcript of interviews is 10 or 11 hours of audiotape for Mr. Krajisnik to listen to. Just listening through once. And he comments, by the way, that sometimes the quality is not terribly good so it is really rather tiring. But if Mr. Krajisnik then has got to listen to 11 hours of B/C/S audiotape just once before he even goes back, or pauses to make any notes, or to think about it or to work on it, this is extremely burdensome for him, and we would remind Your Honour the decision has already been taken. But bearing in mind also that Mr. Krajisnik has to deal with transcripts only by listening to audiotapes, because the decision is that he does not have available to him B/C/S transcripts. This is an enormous burden, and any scheduling of witnesses simply has to take account of that. And it's -- of course I'm sure the Prosecution are aware in general terms that some of these matters have to be dealt with in this way, but it's only actually by discussing then with Mr. Krajisnik and hearing his description of exactly how he has to work and how long it takes and how much time it takes that one does get the full picture of potentially how enormously burdensome and exhausting this process can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I've said enough really to indicate the nature of the difficulty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite clear the point, the issue you pointed out. Well, first of all, the days off. Of course, the Chamber also noted that sometimes the examination of a witness takes less time than the scheduled. That happens. Not only this week, but it happened before as well. So therefore, we gain some time now and then. I'd rather first hear from the parties whether 4th and the 5th would be chosen in such a way that it would cause not too many problems. I did already understand, Mr. Hannis, that it might not cause insurmountable problems. And of course the Chamber would have to consider whether or not to ask compensation, as you wouldn't like, but of course we have to consider it. I put the question to you. Perhaps the Chamber would also like to know more about what exactly is the difference between the 4th and the 5th of November and the 12th, which is a UN holiday, and the 15th until the 19th of November, which is the following week, in which we're not sitting anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can help a little bit on that. So far as the difference between the 4th and the 5th, and let's say the 11th and the 12th are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would rather think about the 12th and the 15th -- or 15th and 16th, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, may I take it in steps, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- first of all. So far as the difference -- because I'll deal with that matter as well. So far as the difference between the 4th and 5th and 11th and 12th are concerned the difference is in effect a week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's it. I mean, it isn't really any more than that because there's no -- in principle there's no greater difficulty. In a sense we use up, if you like, the UN holiday. That may -- I haven't checked this, Your Honour. That can present considerable difficulties as far as access at the UNDU is concerned. So that is something to bear in mind. It's not the easiest of days. I should also say, Your Honour, that planning with two counsel dealing with the process, this schedule of witnesses is not easy, so a great deal of planning has already been done in relation to particular days and weeks, some weeks ahead. But the concern on Mr. Krajisnik's part that a week is a week is a legitimate concern. And we feel it as well, as his Defence team, that really the sooner we are well overdue to get to grips with what's been done and the work that's been done and the material in Pale and elsewhere. So we support Mr. Krajisnik's view that a week earlier is a good thing. So far as the following week is concerned, Your Honour, well, we have -- it is then very disruptive for the Defence, in a way that is probably on balance considerably more disruptive than any consequences of 4th and 5th. We have to then do all kinds of rescheduling and replanning. It's not impossible, but it's very disruptive, both within the Defence team and beyond the Defence team to all sorts of other people. But, well, if we have to do it, we have to do it. But, Your Honour, the witnesses coming along after that break are very heavy witnesses. And when Your Honour says a day is saved, the fact we're not sitting tomorrow saves, if you like, a Loukas day; it saves Ms. Loukas a day in court, because we can rarely afford for both of us to be in court anyway, and Your Honour will notice that we hardly ever are. So it saves a Loukas day. It doesn't save a Stewart day as it happens because I wasn't coming anyway tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course it also saves Mr. Krajisnik day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It does save Mr. Krajisnik's day, of course. That goes without saying, Your Honour. But in relation to the investigators, the important thing, and Mr. Krajisnik's concern is that the investigators should come. But Your Honour I just mention it -- I've mentioned it before. This is a lot of time for us to be involved in the visit of the investigators as well. So we have all the other tasks anyway. Be -- it's not really -- it doesn't solve our problems, Your Honour, to have those two days as non-sitting days and just treat them as the equivalent of two other days when we might not have sat but sit instead. Because this is an extra task for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your point. Mr. Hannis, would it be possible that you provide the Chamber with a little bit more insight on the scheduling for the coming weeks and also flexibility and where you expect to be a bit shorter? Because we have to consider either 11 -- as alternatives if we would agree with 4, 5, we'd see what inconveniences or what risks that would take -- would bring. We'd also consider perhaps the 11th and 12th as alternatives, and also some days in the week of the 15th to the 18th of November. But we'd like to have a bit more insight then in what this would cause in terms of time but also in terms of witnesses that would have to stay over for a weekend unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to the week of November 1st through the 5th, we had three witnesses scheduled who are all coming from the Balkans basically. And they are all talking about the same municipality. So that was part of the reason to have them come that week. We had anticipated that based on how things are going faster than we've been estimating earlier in the trial, that we might have to try and find a fourth witness to fill that week. So if we don't use a fourth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For how much time were they scheduled in chief, these three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 11 and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 11 and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with 60 per cent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would bring us to approximately 18. Well, no. To 20. And that's approximately what we would consider a full week.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you are looking for a fourth witness, of course, we -- at least you could consider to refrain from that. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if we were to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the 11 hours would be brought back to, well, let's say to 8 plus 6 -- plus 4, would be 12 hours, and if we work efficiency, we might be able to do that in three days, which would then create perhaps some extra time without any need to ask for further compensation. Could perhaps the Defence and Prosecution consider whether they think it would be possible to hear these three witnesses scheduled for the 1st until the 5th of November with all discipline which the parties always show to have to deal with it in three days, so the 4th and 5th would become available. That's something to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's extremely disruptive. We're getting to the point where the Defence would rather say forget it. We'll just cope with the situation because -- and Mr. Krajisnik will just have to not come to court for a couple of days. Because this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we see is that at the present pace, we're going through witnesses a bit more quickly, and I take it that the Defence was about to prepare for three witnesses to be heard in court during five days for that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I say that we prepare in a way that we also have to decide who is doing which witnesses. Your Honour, this is an area where the relative small size of the Defence team, in terms of the numbers of counsel available, which is only two of us, is pretty significant, Your Honour. We have to do very careful planning about who does which witness, on what days. Of course we allow for the fact that witnesses go a little bit quicker. We make estimates. But there's a -- it's quite often it's the position is that a particular witness is being brought for a particular day, and we know that, and that is actually important to us in terms of planning. If we didn't know that, the planning which is already difficult would often become absolutely impossible. It's -- I'm not too -- I should say, Your Honour, I'm not too sanguine in any case about simply being able to squeeze witnesses into fewer days we had in mind. Your Honour, I can assure Your Honour if we felt we could do that, routinely and normally, we would do it anyway. We don't have particular incentive or need to be stretching witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It just can't be done sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's not what I am asking. I was just trying to find out whether saving some time on the examination of witnesses in court, which would save two days, either Loukas time or Stewart time, I do understand that there is some -- that there are some -- it would certainly not be easy to reschedule all your preparation activities, but it would -- well, let's say two days counsel time and two days time of Mr. Krajisnik not being in court as well, and -- because you are very much opposed against the idea of finding compensation. Of course, we'll not sit any days extra at another time. But of course it creates other problems. I'm aware of that. Let me say the following: We have a few suggestions now on our table. That is, either the 4th or the 5th, without any compensation, and still to be seen what happens during that week. Three witnesses, two witnesses. At least not a fourth witness. Then we have an option to the 11 and the 12th. I haven't heard about the schedule of that week. I also do understand that the 12th would not be a good day because during UN holidays, as you suggested, there might be no possibility of visitors going to the UN Detention Unit. So that might not be a good solution. Then we have an option of having these investigators to come in the week of the 15th until the 18th of November, which was not very much welcomed, as I understand, especially not by Mr. Krajisnik. I'd like the parties to sit together and to see what these options, what would be possible, and whether you could come to any agreement. If not, of course, the Chamber will have to decide whether we'll seek compensation for not sitting, if it would be the 4th and the 5th of November, or that we would say: No. The investigator should preferably come on the week of the 15th until the 19th of November. So I will ask you to reconsider your positions and to see what solution could be reached at. If there's no solution next Monday or Tuesday, then the Chamber will give a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll meet together and discuss and maybe we can propose something to you tomorrow, Your Honour. I thought as we were talking now of one other possibility, next week has been a difficult week to estimate because -- to estimate because the witness we have coming on Tuesday is a witness who is appearing with regard to a subpoena and there's an issue about whether or not he may be a hostile witness, and it might take a little longer to do his examination-in-chief. Mr. Stewart and I talked about that briefly during the break. There may actually be a little more time next week where we can move up maybe one of the witnesses from the 1st through the 5th of November and put him in at the end of next week. Perhaps the short three-hour witness from Novi Grad that we had scheduled for, I think the 2nd and 3rd of November, we could do on Thursday and Friday of next week. Because Friday the only thing we have is the cross-examination by videolink, and I believe that's not going to take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do see, Mr. Hannis, that you come up with even another option that might bring us a solution. Of course, I haven't heard your response. I don't -- we don't have to hear it now right away. But if you could sit together and see whether you could find any solution for the problem as far as the 5th and -- 4th and 5th of November is concerned. The Chamber will seriously consider that. And that's where we are at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just reiterate that of course one of the things I have to do straight away, haven't had a chance to do since the discussion this morning, is just double-check the availability of the investigators to come on those dates, because I don't want to waste everybody's time without checking that as soon as I possibly can, which I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And perhaps if you introduce that in your conversations with Mr. Hannis. And if they would say we are only available on the week of the 15th of November, we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This issue has been sufficiently dealt with for this moment. We'll hear from the parties at a later stage. Any further issues? Mr. Hannis, procedural ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing other than what I mentioned earlier, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have two additional procedural issues I'd like to raise, one of them in open session, the next one in private session. The Chamber has given it some thought on what the perspectives in this case are, and the Chamber is inclined to issue a scheduling order which would cover the whole of the trial. Of course, it would be not very detailed. The Chamber has considered the matter and has identified a few data which might be important for such a scheduling order, one of them being that the average examination-in-chief of witnesses at this moment is about three hours, each witness; that procedural issues are consuming around 15 per cent of court time. The Chamber would very much like this to be reduced. That the cross-examination is, until now, calculated at about 60 per cent of the examination-in-chief, although frequently takes less. The Chamber also understands that it might be difficult for the Defence to give an estimate on how many witnesses they would call if they would have to present their case. That would mean that, assuming that after the case presentation by the Prosecution, 98 bis motion would be filed, just an assumption. I don't know whether -- you don't have to express any view at this moment, Mr. Stewart. But let's assume that's now and then what happens, isn't it? And if that motion would not be fully granted, then that would mean that the Defence would have to present its case. And experience learns us that the case presentation of a Defence case usually does take 60 per cent or less of the time Prosecution case takes. So that's an assumption. The Chamber is fully aware of that. These are some basics, to some extent assumptions, to some extent data gained by experience, that the Chamber has used to draft a provisional calendar for the year 2005, 2006, which is there for discussion. It would -- just to give you a short outline. It would include the close of the Prosecution case late April, 22nd of April. It would also include that during the months January until March, we'll not sit during three weeks. Then in -- I'll hand it out to you soon. We have a date set then for when the 98 bis motion should be filed, if the Defence intends to do that, how much time would then be given to the Prosecution and when you could expect a decision on such a motion, if it would be filed. This also makes clear that the purpose is not only to impose a time schedule upon the parties but that the Chamber includes itself in this, I would say, disciplinary exercise, disciplinary to say in the terms of discipline rather than disciplinary as it's often used as far as the legal profession is concerned. Then it continues with what would happen if such a motion, if filed, would not be fully granted, what kind of schedule there would be then and what this would mean for the timing of the close of the Defence case, final briefs, closing arguments and when the judgement to be delivered. I hand it out to the parties. It's one A4. Parties are invited next week at an appropriate moment to spend together with the Chamber half an hour on the issue. That would mean that each party can comment on it or make any suggestions, whatever observations the parties would like to make, ten minutes each. And then we have another round of each five minutes. So in half an hour the Chamber gets a clear impression of what position the parties would take in view of such a provisional calendar. That would then probably result in a scheduling order. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask a practical matter at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's some weeks ago, I'm not making a big issue of this, some weeks ago I asked the Prosecution, I think I approached Mr. Harmon direct, actually, but I asked the Prosecution if they would just give us information which I assume they must have, on the progress of their case, the number of witnesses that had been heard, how many hours, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Until now, we have out of approximately 100 scheduled witnesses, we have heard I think 39 or 40. So approximately 60 per cent to be left. So there we are. And I think the Prosecution examination-in-chief took until now close to 130 hours. And on the basis of the use of 89(F) and 92 bis, the Chamber has observed that the balance between the time in court and out of court is a bit different from what it was and has taken that into account as well while drafting this provisional calendar. The Chamber also has considered how much time it approximately takes, and on average, every six weeks in court, so time to sit, not weeks of, six weeks allows us, on the basis of witnesses, three of each three hours in chief, allows us to hear some 20 witnesses in six weeks, sitting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, my request was in effect a simple and innocent one. I think at some point I sent an e-mail to both the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber, because I suppose that either or both would have the necessary information, and in fact of course I know that the Trial Chamber has the information, because I've seen bits of paper with figures and schedules and markings and so on. My request in effect was, whether it comes from the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber, since this is actually simply not tendentious, but it is just data, if there are printouts, if there is information, which I believe there is, that can be produced, that just shows -- I think it's the sort of data which the Trial Chamber is working from. Please may we have it, because the more information we've got -- because actually what we had had in mind over the last two or three weeks was that we were considering what we could propose by way of constructive scheduling. It's the Trial Chamber's primary responsibility, of course. But if we could have as much as this data which presumably can be run off somebody's computer. That would be extremely hem. It's just factual, isn't it? It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's factual. I don't know whether everything is computerised. I can tell you that approximately for the remaining 60 witnesses, or perhaps 62, 63, that number could still vary as well, we're not quite sure about that, we have taken into account approximately 18 weeks of time sitting in court to hear those witnesses. That's more or less in the schedule. Which would bring total examination-in-chief of Prosecution witnesses to approximately 300 hours. And on the basis of what I just said, that would mean some for examination-in-chief of Defence witnesses - of course we do not know that number yet - is calculated at approximately 200 hours in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed. Your Honour, with respect to, all I had in mind was probably the more actual information we have -- the point was really we could do it ourselves over hours and hours. I didn't want Ms. Cmeric, for example, to have to do work that has already been done within the Trial Chamber or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whatever information you would need, tell us. Of course, we have given here on this provisional calendar. You see what the result is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see the result, Your Honour. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What not to sit, how many weeks not to sit, at what date we would expect what to happen. Of course, the schedule for this year is already clear to the parties. One week of November, I think another two weeks off in December. Not sitting the week of the 10th of January. I think we have a late start. That's the second week of 2005. If there are any questions, please -- perhaps the best thing to do is to put them to Mr. Zahar of Chambers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. Perhaps communicating, if I may, because Mr. Harmon in fact is responsible, Mr. Harmon knows what I'm asking for because he has said he will give it to me, and I realise everybody's got work to do. I think my point is that given what the Trial Chamber is now asking us to consider, please, the sooner then Mr. Harmon and his team can now give me the information which we've been discussing over the last few weeks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I can actually use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest that you either first address Mr. Zahar who is very much involved in this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. That's a very helpful suggestion and we shall do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that's -- then we have I think the statistics on how much time that was used until now. It's all there. So it could be -- I mean it's just a matter of computing time. There's one procedural issue I'd like to raise but in private session. Could we turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there seem to be no further procedural issues to be raised at this moment, we would conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had proposed going through the exhibits for a couple of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We could read 92 bis summaries or we could save that for spare time next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether we have any spare time next week. So the Chamber would prefer to have the 92 bis statements read into the transcript, to the extent they are available, and not still be subject to debate between the parties. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know which matter you want to proceed with first. All these outstanding exhibits related to Mr. Medanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, you'd first deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And they were Exhibits 309 through 312, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P309, 92 bis package. Exhibit P310, map, ethnic composition of Kljuc. P311, photograph of post office and community centre. And P312, photograph of Manjaca Detention Centre, dated 30 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Exhibits 309 up until and including 312 are admitted into evidence. Then we still have the exhibits of Witness 144. Is that -- Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement has been redacted in accordance with the Court ruling, and we have that to distribute and replace the other statement now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's under seal. Ms. Loukas, you've seen the new redacted version. No objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, then we have new versions of P Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P325, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to Exhibit P330, the Defence raised an objection. I forwarded after court last night an e-mail to the Defence relating to this document, indicating that it had been seized by the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of February from the archives of the CSB in Banja Luka. I have some further information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This year, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry. 27 February 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I have further information that that seizure on 27 February 1998 was conducted in accordance with a search warrant and that the document arrived at the evidence vault of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 9th of March, 1998. The document purports to be a National Security Centre Banja Luka report, and so its seizure from the CSB archives is consistent with its purported origin. I haven't received a response from the Defence as yet to that further information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, are you already in a position to respond and tell us whether your objection stands? Because then I would say the seal and the signature remain, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, there is still that issue, of course, Your Honour. So my objection still stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is it your position that such a document, if without seal and signature, is not a document that could be admitted into evidence? I mean, I do understand that if a document is signed, that this certainly adds to -- at least could add to the probative value of the document, just assuming that it's not a false signature, et cetera. But a document with signature is more than a document without. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as admissibility is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: On the question of admissibility, Your Honour, of course, in terms of the Rules of the Tribunal relating to evidence, the Tribunal can inform itself in any way it sees fit, and the traditional -- often the traditional Rules of Evidence are dealt with differently here. So the question now becomes one not so much of admissibility but of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, the matter having been reduced now from admissibility to weight, which is not an unimportant matter, I want to stress that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I like to think it's very important, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no reason not to admit into evidence Exhibit P330. So it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Oh, of course there's also the translation, Your Honour, the translation of that particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There were problems about the translation. So I said P330. P330.1 not being included until any problem in respect of translation is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I can just indicate further in relation to translation, Your Honours will recall that I placed on the record that there were translation issues that Ms. Cmeric had identified, significant translation issues. And the delineation of which particular translation issues they were was conveyed by Ms. Cmeric to Mr. Margetts, and the Prosecution is now fully aware of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, will we hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will refer back to CLSS and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you will inform the Chamber. And that would then include 330.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So only P330, the original of this document, is admitted into evidence. Any further procedural issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, other than reading in some of these summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you want to do that after a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems as if there's some ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further issues as far as the Defence is concerned? Mr. Krajisnik, no issues? Okay. Then we'll read into the -- let me just have a look at what time we are. Yes. Could you please start reading some 92 bis, and we'll see -- perhaps we might -- if we come to the next break and we're not finished yet, we might leave the others for next week. But could you give it a start, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll commence with 92 bis summary for a Sanski Most witness, Mr. Besim Islamcevic. That's KRAJ 040. This witness is a Muslim from Podbrijezje in Sanski Most municipality. He attended a number of meetings as a Muslim representative, with Serb authorities, in Sanski Most in 1992. In March and April of 1992, the witness observed soldiers wearing olive-drab coloured uniforms unloading rifles from two olive-drab coloured JNA trucks. He saw the rifles being distributed to Serb inhabitants. The witness observed people wearing Serbian Defence Forces, that is, SOS, insignia in Sanski Most town destroying Muslim shops and establishments. After the Serb authorities in Sanski Most asked for Muslims to surrender their weapons, the witness handed in a pistol. The witness and others heard that the Serb authorities intended to evacuate the Muslim population of Podbrijezje. In the second half of June 1992, the witness and other Muslim representatives requested a meeting with Vladimir Vrkes, president of the SDS in Sanski Most. At the meeting, the Serb representatives explained the steps to be taken to organise the evacuation of Muslims from Podbrijezje. Evacuation procedures included signing a document which transferred all of the signer's property to the SDS. The witness and other Muslims signed a loyalty oath to the Serb authorities. On 27 July 1992, the witness's father-in-law was in an ambulance marked with a visible red cross, on his way to a regular dialysis appointment when the ambulance was stopped by three Serb soldiers. The soldiers asked for any Muslim patients to come out of the ambulance. The patients complied and were taken away. They remain missing. That night, Podbrijezje was attacked. The witness heard shots and saw burning stables and roofs. The next day, the witness told Vrkes about the attack. Vrkes dismissed it as a "fake attack." Some time after this, the witness met again with Vrkes. Vrkes asked the witness to tell him the content of text which the witness, as a Muslim representative, intended to present at a subsequent meeting with UN representatives in Topusko, the subject of which was the reasons the Muslim population had for wanting to leave Sanski Most. The witness read to Vrkes the text he planned to present at the Topusko meeting. It summarised the situation in Sanski Most at the time. In the text, the witness pointed out that up until that time, good relations had existed between Muslims and Serbs, but then 26 mosques in Sanski Most were destroyed. The witness also stated that the Serb authorities were not in a position to ensure security for property, to provide education, to ensure the right to work, to pension schemes, and medical care; in short, the witness was clear that the survival of the Muslim population in Sanski Most was now under threat. After the witness finished reading, Vrkes totally rejected the witness's draft statement and amended it as he saw fit. On 19 August 1992, the witness attended the Topusko meeting as a representative of the Muslim people in Sanski Most. The witness travelled to the meeting with Vrkes, along with others. En route, between the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, Vrkes said, "Soon there will be no border here. All this will be one. All this will be Serb land." At the meeting, the witness presented his revised text to the assembly. Sergio de Mello, the UN representative, asked the Muslims to stay behind at the end of the meeting. The witness told de Mello that there was a lot of disturbance in Sanski Most, such as lootings and destruction of religious buildings and everything else that had been redacted by Vrkes from the speech the witness gave during the meeting. The witness reported two major attacks on the Trnovo and Hrustovo local communes. A large number of civilians had been killed in Hrustovo. De Mello replied that he knew about Hrustovo. De Mello also stated that the UN would not assist in the movement of the population of Sanski Most. The witness describes the obligations of the Muslims to pay outstanding taxes and utility bills and to receive certificates from banks to prove that they had no outstanding debts before the Serb municipal authorities would issue certificates permitting them to leave Sanski Most. The witness describes convoys of Muslims that he saw leaving Sanski Most. None of them left voluntarily, although they were forced to sign papers that stated otherwise. One convoy consisted of 1.080 Muslim refugees from Mahala who had taken refuge in Podbrijezje after Mahala was shelled and set afire. The Serb army and the chief of police rounded up the 1.080 people, expelled them from Podbrijezje. Another convoy consisted of Muslim citizens from part of the right bank of Sanski Most. In early September 1992, the witness and other Muslim representatives met with Vrkes and members of the Serb Crisis Staff. They determined that they would not -- need at least 15 to 20 buses to evacuate the Muslims from Sanski Most. The witness describes -- Sorry. This was a mistake. They would need at least 15 to 20 buses. Apologies. The witness describes the convoy of lorries and buses carrying approximately 2.500 people, which left Sanski Most, escorted by civilian and military police, on or about 2 September 1992. The Muslims were not leaving voluntarily; they were leaving in order to save themselves and their children. The witness describes his meeting with Karadzic and Rasula on 25 September 1992 in Banja Luka. Karadzic encouraged the witness to help the Serb authorities to establish themselves. Karadzic explained to the witness that the Serbs would wage war and that the Muslims would work. Karadzic explained that, after a Serb state was established, those who wanted to remain and work would be allowed to remain, and those who did not would be allowed to leave. Karadzic told Rasula: "Let them work and we will wage war." Throughout the rest of 1992, the witness and other Muslims who remained in Sanski Most performed work duty tasks assigned to them by Serb authorities, including the removal of rubble from sites of destroyed mosques. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that it would be time for another summary to be read, or two short ones. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have some short ones, and for the sake of the court reporter, I'm going to go out of order and the next one I'm going to read is a witness from Brcko, with protective measures. This is Witness KRAJ 220.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the protective measures were?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This was a witness from the Jelisic case and the protective measures were carried over from that case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was -- pseudonym, Madam Registrar? Could you please check. Because witnesses who have testified -- no. It's 92 bis, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he had a pseudonym in the Jelisic case and we requested a pseudonym in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only protective measure. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness was taken from his home in Brcko by Serb soldiers on 6 May 1992 to the Laser bus company and detained there for two days until transferred to Luka Camp. There were approximately 400 Muslims and Croats detained at Luka while the witness was there. Goran Jelisic said he was the boss at Luka. Goran Jelisic killed several civilian detainees between 8 May and 18 May 1992 at Luka. The witness personally saw two of those killings. He had to carry a number of dead bodies and clean up the area where the killings took place. He saw piles of dead bodies and notes that a number were thrown into the Sava River. The witness was later taken to Batkovic camp and detained there until he was exchanged on the 12th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The summary said on or about the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On or about 12 October, 1992. Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That concludes that summary. Do you want to take a break or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact if you could read another one, we'll then finish for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will read another -- I will read another one from Brcko. Witness with a pseudonym. This was KRAJ 436. The witness provides evidence of killing and sexual assault in June 1992, when she was aged 13 years. On 21 June 1992, the witness and her family were asleep on the ground floor of her house. A group of soldiers identified themselves as "the police" and ordered the door opened. The family complied and the soldiers came into the house. All of the soldiers were in uniform and were armed. The witness saw a soldier beat and then shoot her grandmother, killing her. The witness was taken out of the house and told by the soldiers that the remainder of her family had also been executed. This information later turned out to be incorrect, but the witness believed that the rest of her family had in fact been killed. The witness was then forced to get into a car with a member of the Bosnian Serb forces. During the drive, the man told the witness, "You have to blame your Alija for this." The man took the witness to an apartment in Brcko, where he detained her for two or three days. At the apartment, the man sexually assaulted the witness several times. That concludes this summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. We'll then conclude not only for the day but for the week as well. We'll not sit tomorrow. I wish the Defence a lot of strength in mastering the EDS system, CaseMap and LiveNote because that's on your programme for tomorrow as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've already done it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Ms. Loukas is the victim for tomorrow. Yes. Well, I see both Mr. Krajisnik and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wish to bring to your attention that Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a moment there I thought you had forgotten about me, Your Honour. I would kindly like to address the Trial Chamber, but in a closed session, in relation to an item that you referred to a moment ago where you turned into a private session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session. I at the same time look at the clock. We might not have any more than five to seven minutes.
